title: CURE: Consistency-under-Unified Semantic Regularization for Generalized Category Discovery
one_liner: CURE solves the conflict between forcing features far apart and keeping similar examples close by learning known categories first, then extending to new ones with a unified semantic anchor.
lead: When a model learns categories from labeled examples, it can discover new unlabeled categories by grouping similar features. But the two standard objectives that guide this learning tug in opposite directions: one pushes all features to spread evenly across space, while the other pulls similar examples together. CURE splits this into two stages—learning known categories precisely first, then carefully extending to unknowns—so both objectives work toward the same goal.

problem.h2: Two objectives pulling in opposite directions
paras: A beginner learning new categories might train a model on labeled data (apples, oranges) and hope it groups unlabeled data (unknown fruits) correctly. The standard recipe uses two forces: uniformity (spread features out evenly so the model doesn't cluster everything in one spot, because a model that groups everything in one corner learns nothing) and consistency (keep similar examples close together in feature space, which is what makes them cluster into categories). These forces conflict. Uniformity spreads everything apart, but consistency wants to bunch similar things together. When both run at the same time, the model gets stuck—it cannot spread uniformly while grouping coherently, so known categories blur and the unlabeled categories scatter randomly.

The model learns messy, incoherent representations where known and unknown categories overlap and mix. Performance on known categories drops, and grouping of unlabeled data into real categories fails.

callout.html: Learn known categories in isolation first with their own fixed anchors, then extend carefully to unknowns using only consistency, with a unified semantic guide to prevent information loss.

panels.title: 1. The problem
panels.caption: Labeled apples and oranges cluster loosely; unlabeled fruits scatter.

panels.title: 2. Uniformity pulls apart
panels.caption: Spread everything evenly in feature space. But now similar apples are far from each other.

panels.title: 3. Consistency wants clustering
panels.viz_args: Apple + Apple bundle; Orange + Orange bundle; Unknown alone.
panels.caption: Pull similar examples close. But uniformity resists clustering, creating conflict.

panels.title: 4. CURE: Stage one, anchored learning
panels.caption: Learn apples and oranges around fixed prototypes without uniformity interference.

panels.title: 5. Stage two, consistent extension
panels.caption: Unlabeled fruits find their nearest labeled category cluster using consistency only.

steps.text: Align each labeled category (apple, orange) with a learnable anchor point in feature space.
Skip the uniformity objective; train only on consistency and semantic alignment to prototypes.
Compute an energy measure that finds shared traits across all categories, preventing the loss of information.
In stage two, pull unlabeled examples toward the nearest known cluster using consistency alone.
Known categories stay sharp; unlabeled groups form clean clusters near them instead of scattering randomly.

paras: CURE changes the training recipe: it removes uniformity (the even-spread force) during category learning, instead anchoring known categories to fixed prototype points. This prevents the conflict that made both objectives fail. In the second stage, only consistency pulls unlabeled data toward known clusters, with a unified semantic guide keeping shared information intact.

hidden.h2: Semantic Exploration Energy: shared meaning across all categories
hidden.name: Semantic Exploration Energy
paras: As the model learns, different categories develop their own feature patterns. If prototypes (the anchor points for each category) push too far apart, the model can forget traits that multiple categories share—like color, size, or texture. Semantic Exploration Energy measures how much shared information (patterns that appear across multiple categories) remains intact, preventing that loss.

The paper estimates this energy by computing how close each unlabeled example sits to the weighted average of all known category prototypes. High energy means unlabeled examples land in regions tied to multiple known categories; low energy means they land in isolated pockets with no shared thread back.

heat.caption: Darker means higher semantic energy: closer to multiple known prototypes.

reads.html: Semantic Exploration Energy is a score that tells you how deeply an unlabeled example is rooted in the shared territory of known categories. High energy means it sits in a zone that speaks to multiple labeled groups; low energy means it is stranded in an isolated pocket.

The Semantic Exploration Energy mechanism computes a weighted proximity measure between unlabeled samples and a unified center derived from all known prototypes, keeping information intact when prototypes are pushed apart.

mechanism.h2: Why splitting into stages solves the conflict
paras: In the first stage, the model learns known categories as anchored clusters around fixed prototype points. It uses only consistency (pull similar labeled examples together) and semantic alignment (make each example sit near its true category's prototype). It skips uniformity entirely, so the model can form tight, coherent clusters for apples and oranges without external pressure to spread them out, because there is no competing force pulling in the opposite direction. Known categories crystallize.

In the second stage, the model extends to unlabeled groups using only consistency: pull each unlabeled example toward whichever known cluster it resembles. The Semantic Exploration Energy mechanism adds a unified anchor—a point in feature space that represents the common ground across all known categories. This anchor pulls unlabeled examples toward the center of the known categories rather than letting them scatter. The result: unlabeled groups form as coherent extensions of known ones, grouped by real similarity, not pushed apart by a conflicting spread-it-wide force.

stages.s: Labeled data (apples, oranges) + unlabeled data (unknown fruits)
Learn anchored representations: consistency + semantic alignment, no uniformity
Compute semantic overlap via shared center point
Extend to unknowns: pull toward nearest known cluster
Sharp known categories + coherent unlabeled groupings

math.h2: The consistency and semantic alignment loss
math.words: Total loss equals consistency loss (pull similar pairs close) plus semantic alignment loss (pull each example toward its known prototype) plus the unified semantic energy term (pull toward the shared center).
symbols: loss that pulls similar examples in a batch close together
loss that pulls each labeled example toward its category prototype
loss that keeps unlabeled examples anchored to the shared center of all known prototypes
a weight controlling how strongly semantic energy pulls on novel examples

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a batch has 10 apple examples, 8 orange examples, 6 unknown examples.
Consistency loss: apple-apple pairs (28 possible) contribute 28 units; orange-orange pairs (10 possible) contribute 10 units. Total: 38.

Semantic align loss: each of the 18 labeled examples is pulled toward its prototype. Apple examples pull toward apple-prototype (distance 0.8 each) = 14.4; orange examples (distance 0.6 each) = 10.8. Total: 25.2.
Semantic energy: 6 unknowns pull toward the center (average of prototypes). Center distance 1.2 each = 7.2. With lambda=0.5: 3.6.
Total loss: 38 + 25.2 + 3.6 = 66.8. Removing uniformity prevents conflict; removing it would lower loss initially but ruin category coherence.

math.note: The key is removing uniformity and adding the semantic energy anchor; this keeps unlabeled examples from drifting into incoherent space.

bars.h2: Performance: known categories vs. unlabeled groups

charts.title: Naive approach (both objectives)
charts.note: Uniformity and consistency conflict, so both objectives half-work. Known categories blur; unlabeled groups scatter randomly.

charts.title: CURE (two-stage, semantic anchor)
charts.note: Stage one crystallizes known categories. Stage two anchors unlabeled ones coherently. Known and unlabeled performance converges.

items.b: Prototypes too close or too far.
items.html: If known category prototypes are placed too near each other, unlabeled examples cannot distinguish which known cluster to join, because there is no clear separating space. If too far apart, unlabeled groups land in gaps with weak connection. The semantic energy anchor helps by pulling toward the center, but prototype initialization matters.

items.b: Unlabeled data from categories outside the known set.
items.html: If most unlabeled data comes from categories not in the labeled set, the semantic energy center gives weak guidance. Unlabeled clusters form far from known ones, and the shared thread weakens.

items.b: Stage one with poor labeled data quality.
items.html: If labeled examples are noisy or unbalanced (far more apples than oranges), their prototypes are off-center. Stage two propagates that error to unlabeled groups via consistency.
With clean labeled data and balanced representation, two-stage learning with semantic anchoring keeps known categories sharp and unlabeled groups coherent.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small category discovery experiment: 5 labeled categories (e.g., 50 images each from CIFAR: airplane, automobile, bird, cat, dog) and 5 unlabeled categories (truck, horse, ship, frog, deer) treated as unlabeled. Train CURE in two stages on the labeled split. Then measure accuracy on the unlabeled split by assigning each image to its nearest known cluster. Compare known vs. unlabeled accuracy, and compute the gap. The demo should show that the gap is small (unlabeled groups coherently cluster near known ones) while both accuracies remain high.
demo.metric_eq: Gap = accuracy_known - accuracy_novel. CURE should achieve gap < 10%, while naive two-objective methods achieve gap > 20%.
demo.closing: The irreducible proof: when stage one crystallizes known categories and stage two uses semantic anchoring, unlabeled groups align coherently with known structure, not scatter randomly.
